content.title: About
content.content: Cocoa powder is made from roasted, ground cocoa beans (Theobroma cacao) after most of the cocoa butter has been pressed out. It is a dark brown, bitter, unsweetened powder with an intense chocolate flavor. Cocoa powder is used in baking, desserts, hot cocoa, smoothies, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Natural cocoa powder is acidic and lighter in color, while Dutch-processed (alkalized) cocoa is treated to neutralize acidity and is darker and milder.
Cocoa beans come from the seeds of the cacao tree, which is native to tropical regions of the Americas.
Cocoa naturally contains theobromine, a mild stimulant related to caffeine.
Unsweetened cocoa powder is very bitter, unlike sweetened drinking chocolate mixes.
Cocoa is rich in plant compounds called flavanols, though processing can reduce them.

items.title: Contains flavanols
items.content: Cocoa contains flavanols, plant compounds with antioxidant properties that are being studied.

items.title: Provides magnesium and iron
items.content: Cocoa provides magnesium and iron, which support muscle function and oxygen transport.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Cocoa powder contributes fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Intense flavor with little sugar
items.content: Unsweetened cocoa adds chocolate flavor without added sugar.

items.title: Caffeine and theobromine
items.content: Cocoa contains stimulants that may cause restlessness, trouble sleeping, or a fast heartbeat in sensitive people, children, and during pregnancy if eaten in large amounts.

items.title: Heavy metals
items.content: Some cocoa products contain traces of cadmium and lead, so eat cocoa in moderation and choose reputable brands.

items.title: Toxic to dogs
items.content: Cocoa and chocolate are toxic to dogs and cats because of theobromine, so keep them away from pets.

items.title: Allergies, migraines, and added sugar
items.content: Cocoa can trigger reactions or migraines in some people, and sweetened cocoa mixes can be high in sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cocoa powder can be sifted into cake, brownie, cookie, and pancake batters, stirred into oatmeal or smoothies, or whisked with hot milk and a little sweetener to make hot cocoa. Use unsweetened cocoa powder when you want to control the sugar. Dutch-processed and natural cocoa behave differently in baking recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cocoa powder in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place, where it keeps for a year or longer. Keep it away from moisture and strong odors. Discard cocoa that has clumped, smells musty, or shows mold.
